items.q: A 68-year-old patient suddenly develops weakness and sensory loss predominantly affecting the left leg and foot, with relative sparing of the face and arm. Urinary incontinence and mild apathy are noted. Which artery is most likely occluded?
items.exp: The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial aspect of the hemisphere representing the leg and foot on the motor and sensory homunculi, plus the paracentral lobule controlling micturition.
r: Correct. Right ACA infarction affects medial motor and sensory cortex for the contralateral leg and micturition center.
Incorrect. MCA stroke predominantly impairs face and upper extremity strength.
Incorrect. Left MCA stroke causes right sided face/arm weakness and aphasia.
Incorrect. PCA infarction causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia.
items.kp: Anterior cerebral artery occlusion causes contralateral leg and foot weakness, sensory loss, and urinary incontinence.

items.q: A 54-year-old patient presents with sudden severe right hemiparesis and hemisensory loss affecting face and arm much more than leg, accompanied by global aphasia. Which vascular territory is infarcted?
items.exp: The left (dominant) middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral cortex including Broca and Wernicke areas and the motor homunculus for face and arm.
r: Correct. Left MCA stroke causes right face/arm weakness, sensory deficit, and aphasia.
Incorrect. Left ACA stroke causes leg greater than arm weakness.
Incorrect. Right MCA stroke causes left hemiparesis and hemineglect.
Incorrect. Basilar artery occlusion produces bilateral brainstem signs or locked-in state.
items.kp: Dominant middle cerebral artery stroke produces contralateral face and arm weakness along with expressive or receptive aphasia.

items.q: Which arterial segment is the most common anatomical site for saccular (berry) intracranial aneurysms?
items.exp: The anterior communicating artery junction is the most frequent site of intracranial berry aneurysms, accounting for approximately 30-35% of all cases.
r: Correct. Anterior communicating artery is the most common berry aneurysm location.
Incorrect. Basilar bifurcation accounts for approximately 5-10% of aneurysms.
Incorrect. MCA bifurcation accounts for about 20-25%.
Incorrect. PICA aneurysms are less frequent.
items.kp: The anterior communicating artery junction is the most common site of intracranial saccular berry aneurysms.

items.q: An aneurysm arising at the junction of the internal carotid artery and posterior communicating artery commonly compresses which adjacent cranial nerve, presenting with painful ptosis and pupillary dilation?
items.exp: The oculomotor nerve runs directly adjacent to the junction of the internal carotid and posterior communicating artery. PCOM aneurysms compress CN III, causing painful third nerve palsy with an unreactive dilated pupil.
r: Correct. PCOM aneurysm classically causes painful oculomotor nerve palsy with pupillomotor involvement.
Incorrect. CN IV runs more laterally along the tentorial edge.
Incorrect. CN VI runs within Dorello canal in the cavernous sinus.
Incorrect. V1 provides corneal sensation.
items.kp: Posterior communicating artery aneurysm classically produces painful third cranial nerve palsy with pupillary involvement.

items.q: Which vessels directly form the posterior anastomotic link between the carotid system and the vertebrobasilar circulation in the Circle of Willis?
items.exp: The paired posterior communicating arteries connect the internal carotid arteries anteriorly with the posterior cerebral arteries of the vertebrobasilar circulation posteriorly.
r: Correct. Posterior communicating arteries bridge internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries.
Incorrect. Anterior communicating artery bridges bilateral anterior cerebral arteries.
Incorrect. Superior cerebellar arteries arise from the basilar artery below the PCA.
Incorrect. Anterior choroidal artery arises from ICA to supply posterior limb of internal capsule.
items.kp: Posterior communicating arteries provide the critical collateral bridge between anterior and posterior cerebral circulations.

items.q: Occlusion of the lenticulostriate arteries arising from the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery classically produces which clinical stroke syndrome?
o: Pure motor hemiparesis from posterior limb internal capsule infarction
items.exp: Lenticulostriate arteries supply the basal ganglia and the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Lacunar infarction here produces pure motor stroke involving face, arm, and leg equally.
r: Correct. Lenticulostriate stroke damages the posterior limb of internal capsule, causing pure motor hemiparesis.
Incorrect. Bitemporal hemianopia results from chiasm compression.
Incorrect. Wallenberg syndrome stems from PICA or vertebral occlusion.
Incorrect. Broca aphasia requires cortical infarction.
items.kp: Lenticulostriate arterial occlusion causes lacunar strokes in the internal capsule, manifesting as pure motor hemiparesis.

items.q: Watershed (borderzone) cerebral infarctions occurring after profound systemic hypotension most commonly affect the junction between which two arterial territories?
o: Anterior cerebral and middle cerebral artery territories
Posterior cerebral and anterior inferior cerebellar territories
Posterior communicating and anterior choroidal territories
items.exp: The cortical watershed zone between the ACA and MCA territories is located along the high convexity, producing proximal arm and leg weakness termed 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome.
r: Correct. ACA-MCA borderzone is the most vulnerable cortical watershed territory during systemic hypoperfusion.
Incorrect. Posterior circulation vessels have rich collateral anastomoses.
Incorrect. Cerebellar borderzones are less frequently symptomatic.
Incorrect. These are proximal conducting branches.
items.kp: Watershed infarctions occur at ACA-MCA and MCA-PCA border zones following profound hypotensive episodes, causing man-in-a-barrel weakness.

items.q: Which dural venous sinus courses along the attached margin of the falx cerebri to terminate at the confluence of sinuses (torcular Herophili)?
items.exp: The superior sagittal sinus runs in the superior border of the falx cerebri from crista galli to the confluence of sinuses, receiving arachnoid granulations and bridging veins.
r: Correct. Superior sagittal sinus occupies the upper convex margin of the falx cerebri.
Incorrect. Inferior sagittal sinus runs in the free inferior margin of falx cerebri.
Incorrect. Straight sinus forms at junction of falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli.
Incorrect. Cavernous sinus lies on either side of the sella turcica.
items.kp: Superior sagittal sinus runs along the superior attachment of the falx cerebri and empties into the confluence of sinuses.

items.q: A patient presents with severe proptosis, chemosis, and progressive ophthalmoplegia affecting CN III, IV, and VI, accompanied by forehead numbness. Thrombosis of which vascular structure explains these findings?
items.exp: The cavernous sinus encloses CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI, along with the internal carotid artery. Cavernous sinus thrombosis produces proptosis, chemosis, and painful ophthalmoplegia.
r: Correct. Cavernous sinus thrombosis compresses CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI traversing its walls and lumen.
Incorrect. Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis causes headache, seizures, and elevated ICP.
Incorrect. Sigmoid sinus thrombosis causes mastoid tenderness (Griesinger sign).
Incorrect. Internal jugular thrombosis impairs systemic venous outflow.
items.kp: Cavernous sinus thrombosis presents with chemosis, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia due to involvement of CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI.

items.q: What is the primary anatomical origin of the posterior cerebral arteries?
items.exp: The basilar artery ascends along the ventral pons and terminates at the upper pontine border by bifurcating into the paired posterior cerebral arteries.
r: Correct. The basilar artery terminates by dividing into both posterior cerebral arteries.
Incorrect. Internal carotid gives off ACA, MCA, PCOM, and anterior choroidal.
Incorrect. Vertebral arteries unite to form the basilar artery.
Incorrect. AICA is a branch of the lower basilar trunk.
items.kp: The posterior cerebral arteries originate as the terminal bifurcation branches of the basilar artery.
